The memorandum of understanding (MoU) was signed Saturday in Mogadishu by Transport and Civil Aviation Minister Mohamed Farah Nuh, Somali Civil Aviation Authority Director General Ahmed Moallim Hassan and Kamil Alawadhi, IATA’s regional vice president for Africa and the Middle East. advertisements Under the agreement, the Somali Civil Aviation Authority will recognize the IATA Operational Safety Audit (IOSA) and the IATA Safety Audit for Ground Operations (ISAGO) as acceptable means of compliance with national regulations, complementing its own safety oversight functions. The programs will complement, rather than replace, the authority’s own regulatory and safety oversight functions. “Global safety standards are the cornerstone of efficient and safe operations. Through this MoU, we will work with the Somali CAA towards the continuous improvement of safety standards, promote the adoption of industry best practices, and foster a culture of safety across the aviation sector. This partnership reflects our mutual dedication to advancing aviation safety for the benefit of passengers, operators and the wider aviation industry in Somalia and Africa,” said Kamil Alawadhi, IATA’s Regional Vice President for Africa and Middle East. IOSA is an internationally recognized audit system designed to assess an airline’s operational management and control systems. More than 450 airlines are currently listed on the IOSA registry, and all IATA member airlines are required to maintain IOSA registration. ISAGO applies similar standardized oversight to companies providing ground-handling services at airports. IATA says the program is intended to reduce operational risks, improve consistency in ground handling and limit duplication between audits conducted by airlines, airports and regulators. The agreement forms part of IATA’s Focus Africa initiative, which includes efforts to improve aviation safety, infrastructure, connectivity and regulatory standards across the continent. The agreement signed in Mogadishu comes as authorities continue rebuilding a civil aviation system that was severely weakened after the collapse of the central government in 1991. The country has gradually reestablished national control over aviation functions, including management of Somali airspace and regulatory oversight of airlines and airports. somalia.content: Families fleeing Somalia crises find bleak prospects in Dadaab refugee camps - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Families fleeing Somalia crises find bleak prospects in Dadaab refugee camps Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Tuesday October 20, 2026 Nurto fled conflict in Baidoa and is struggling to support her seven children in Dadaab refugee camps/Ahmed Abdulahi/Ergo Families fleeing adversity in different parts of southern Somalia have been arriving in Kenya’s Dadaab refugee camps, where they find themselves with no means of making a living nor aid or support. They include families fleeing conflict in Baidoa, house demolitions by the Somali government in Mogadishu, and drought in their home areas. advertisements The new arrivals say they have received no reception support, shelter, or other forms of aid. Some are staying with relatives already struggling to make ends meet, while others have settled on their own on vacant land in Dadaab’s Ifo-2 camp. They lack food, housing, toilets and other basic services. Nurto Mohamed Ali, who arrived in Ifo-2 on 20 August, said her family had received no assistance and was struggling to meet basic needs. She is staying with relatives who arrived earlier. “Neighbours collect maize and cooking oil for us. That is how we are surviving now,” she said. “We have children who need food and bedding, but we have nothing to give them.” Nurto fled ongoing conflict in Baidoa between federal government forces and those loyal to the former South West State administration. She was a farmer raising her family on their two-hectare plot of land in Baidoa. Separated from her husband, she receives no support from him and is the sole income earner. In the refugee camp now, her seven children often go to bed hungry because she lacks food. They occupy a shelter made from plastic sheets, cloth and thorny branches in the yard of a relatives’ home – a household of 10. The days reach a scorching 37°C and the rainy season has begun. Nurto and her older children have to sleep outside without bedding while the youngest children cram themselves into the hut. Nurto said they had expected to receive assistance on arrival, including refugee registration cards, household items, and a house. She has received nothing. “We have no proper house, and even the people who arrived before us do not have one. The shelter situation is very difficult. We sleep on pieces of cloth and a small, broken mat,” she said. Other vulnerable new arrivals, including older people, people with disabilities, women and children, are finding no formal help in the camp, where some walk around daily asking more established residents for food. Hawo Mohamed Ali, her disabled husband, and their 10 children arrived in Ifo-2 on 1 August. They fled Mogadishu’s Hodan district after the government demolished their house, saying the land belonged to the state. They had lived in the house for 34 years without having formal land ownership documents. She said losing the home made it impossible for her family to remain in Mogadishu. “When we left and went outside, we found our land fenced off and surrounded by a wall,” she told Radio Ergo. “We were told the land would be measured and returned to us. Our houses were demolished using bulldozers, and we thought the land would be given back. Later, we were told it was government land and that we had to leave.” The demolition left Hawo’s family homeless and they decided their only option was to seek refuge in Dadaab. In Mogadishu, she earned a living selling meat and watermelon in local markets. In the refugee camp, however, they have not been registered and haven’t received aid cards or assistance. She looked for laundry work, but the jobs are irregular, so she has to ask others for help with food for her children. She lacks firewood and containers for collecting water. “The children’s father is disabled, and life is very difficult for us. My children are still young and have nothing here. We left our home and came to a place we do not know,” said Hawo, adding that the conditions in Dadaab were far worse than she had expected. The chairman of Hagardera camp, Khalif Dhubow Jelle, said the hardship facing new arrivals from Somalia had been brought to the attention of humanitarian agencies in the camps, but no effective response had followed. He recorded nearly 250 families having arrived from southern Somalia in the past three months. “Their living conditions are extremely poor. It is also the rainy season, yet these people have no shelter or place to stay. They are sitting in the open and have no food or water,” he said. The new arrivals are joining a refugee population already struggling with difficult living conditions because of reduced humanitarian aid and wider economic hardship across the camps. Attending Kenya’s Mashujaa Day celebrations as President William Ruto’s guest of honour, Abiy emphasized the longstanding partnership between the two countries, highlighting cooperation in electricity, telecommunications, trade and regional connectivity. Yet beyond the diplomatic celebrations, the visit coincided with growing tensions involving Somalia, whose internal political crisis has begun complicating its relations with both Ethiopia and Kenya. Although Abiy’s visit was officially centered on Kenya’s Mashujaa Day celebrations and bilateral cooperation, it unfolded against a backdrop of growing regional tensions involving Somalia. The visit did not publicly establish a common Ethiopian and Kenyan position on the Somali crisis, but it brought renewed attention to the strategic importance of their partnership as both countries navigate increasingly complicated relations with Mogadishu. The significance of Ethiopia’s relationship with Kenya extends beyond bilateral cooperation. Both countries have invested considerable military and diplomatic resources in Somalia’s stabilization, particularly in efforts to contain Al Shabaab and prevent insecurity from spreading across their borders. However, Somalia’s confrontation between its federal government and regional political actors is creating disagreements over the responsibilities of neighbouring countries. For Ethiopia, the challenge is to maintain its commitment to Somalia’s security without becoming involved in political disputes that could undermine its wider regional interests. The immediate source of tension lies in Somalia’s South West State, where the removal of former regional president Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen in March 2026 failed to produce a lasting political settlement. Instead, confrontations between his supporters and forces aligned with the federal government have continued, exposing deeper disagreements over regional autonomy and the distribution of political authority. By October 19, forces loyal to Laftagareen reportedly controlled five towns in the Bay region, including Buurhakaba, Qansaxdheere and Dinsoor, complicating Mogadishu’s efforts to consolidate authority. The conflict is particularly consequential because the South West State includes territories where Ethiopian forces have maintained a security presence for years. According to Somali Guardian reporting published on October 19 , Somali federal authorities requested Ethiopian military assistance against forces aligned with Laftagareen, but Ethiopian commanders declined to participate in what they considered an internal political confrontation. Although the reported exchange has not been independently confirmed, it illustrates a fundamental question concerning foreign military involvement in Somalia: whether security assistance intended to confront common threats should extend to supporting the federal government in disputes over domestic political authority. For Ethiopia, the issue has acquired additional importance following the transition from the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia, ATMIS, to the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia, AUSSOM, which commenced on January 1, 2025. Under United Nations Security Council Resolution 2767 , the successor mission was authorized to support Somali forces against Al Shabaab, protect civilians and facilitate the gradual transfer of security responsibilities to Somali institutions. Its mandate also encompasses security support for political processes, but does not provide unrestricted authority to determine the outcome of internal political disputes. The transition brought renewed attention to the distinction between Ethiopian troops operating under African Union arrangements and those deployed through separate bilateral security understandings. This distinction matters because forces assigned to AUSSOM operate within a defined multinational framework, while deployments outside that structure depend on separate arrangements with Somalia. In its December 2025 communiqué , the African Union Peace and Security Council explicitly acknowledged Ethiopia and Uganda for deploying additional troops under bilateral arrangements. Their presence cannot therefore be understood solely through AUSSOM’s command structure. Ethiopia’s longstanding involvement in Somalia has primarily been driven by the need to prevent Al Shabaab from developing secure operating areas near Ethiopian territory. The group’s ability to exploit instability and threaten communities across borders makes developments in Somalia directly relevant to Ethiopia’s national security. Ethiopian military operations and participation in successive African Union missions have consequently contributed to a broader effort to contain threats before they reach Ethiopian territory. The South West State remains especially important because the Bay and Bakool regions form part of the wider security environment connected to Ethiopia’s eastern frontier. Participation in Somalia’s internal political confrontations, however, would expose Ethiopia to different risks. Military intervention could associate Ethiopian forces with one Somali political faction, weaken relationships with local communities and transform a defined security commitment into an extended responsibility for political outcomes. Even a successful intervention would not necessarily resolve disagreements concerning federal authority and regional political representation. Somalia’s domestic disputes require political settlements that military involvement by neighbouring countries cannot independently deliver. This position should not be confused with opposition to Somalia’s federal government. Addis Ababa and Mogadishu continue to maintain diplomatic relations and share an interest in preventing renewed militant expansion. Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s September 29 visit to Addis Ababa , during which he discussed bilateral relations and regional security with Abiy Ahmed, demonstrated the continued importance of diplomatic engagement despite existing disagreements. Those disagreements nevertheless have a deeper history. The January 2024 memorandum of understanding between Ethiopia and Somaliland, which addressed potential Ethiopian maritime access, produced a significant confrontation with Mogadishu over sovereignty and territorial integrity. Somalia regarded the arrangement as an infringement on its sovereignty, while Ethiopia viewed access to the sea as an important strategic and economic objective. The dispute contributed to Somalia’s closer security engagement with Egypt, which already maintained long winded Nile disagreements with Ethiopia. The December 2024 Ankara Declaration , facilitated by Türkiye, helped restore diplomatic engagement by reaffirming mutual respect for sovereignty and acknowledging the possibility of mutually beneficial maritime arrangements under Somalia’s sovereign authority. Nevertheless, restoring diplomatic communication did not eliminate competing regional security calculations. Egypt’s expanding security engagement with Somalia and its prospective contribution to AUSSOM have introduced further sensitivity into discussions about troop deployments. The African Union’s June 2025 negotiations with troop-contributing countries included Ethiopia and Egypt, demonstrating that both countries were considered within the mission’s institutional arrangements. In December 2025, the African Union also acknowledged Egypt’s preparations for deployment while emphasizing the need to prevent security gaps during the transition. Political endorsement, negotiated contributions and actual troop deployments, however, remain distinct stages. For Ethiopia, any substantial expansion of Egyptian forces near areas where Ethiopian troops operate would raise operational questions, particularly given the unresolved Nile dispute. Careful coordination would be essential to prevent competing strategic interests from complicating counterterrorism operations. Kenya faces a related challenge arising from Somalia’s domestic political confrontation. Laftagareen’s presence in Kenya following his removal has generated criticism from Somali officials. On October 19, Somalia’s parliamentary speaker, Abdikadir Mohamed Nur Jama, reportedly accused individuals residing in Kenya of involvement in activities connected to the conflict and questioned the alleged protection they received. The reporting did not establish evidence supporting those allegations, and Kenyan authorities had not publicly responded at the time. Hosting Somali political figures does not independently demonstrate Kenyan government support for their military activities. Nairobi must balance its diplomatic responsibilities and continued cooperation with Mogadishu against its own legal and national security considerations. The consequences of Somali instability for Kenya are also economic. The Lamu Port South Sudan Ethiopia Transport corridor, LAPSSET, represents an important regional infrastructure initiative intended to expand commercial connectivity and diversify access to maritime trade. Its security is connected to conditions in northern and coastal Kenya, where Al Shabaab has demonstrated the ability to threaten personnel and transport infrastructure. On September 19, 2026, suspected militants attacked Kenyan military personnel patrolling part of the corridor in Garissa. No casualties were reported, but the incident illustrated the security demands associated with protecting strategic infrastructure. Although these attacks cannot be directly attributed to the South West State’s political crisis, prolonged instability in Somalia could place additional pressure on counterterrorism operations and create opportunities for militant expansion. For Kenya, preserving security cooperation with Somalia therefore carries implications for domestic security, investment and regional transport connectivity. Ethiopia shares an interest in protecting these connections, which could strengthen economic integration and provide additional commercial routes. Against this background, the partnership between Addis Ababa and Nairobi offers continuity. Cooperation in electricity transmission, telecommunications and transport has created practical interests that extend beyond individual political disagreements. During his October 20 visit , Abiy emphasized Ethiopia’s electricity exports to Kenya, Safaricom’s presence in Ethiopia and growing commercial connections. Their importance becomes greater as Ethiopia confronts renewed tensions with Eritrea, instability in northern Ethiopia and unresolved strategic disagreements with Egypt. The October 2026 escalation in Tigray and tensions with Eritrea demonstrate the competing pressures confronting Addis Ababa. Strong relations with Kenya provide an additional channel for diplomatic consultation without requiring both governments to adopt identical policies toward Somalia. The coming months will test whether the three countries can prevent Somalia’s internal confrontation from developing into a wider regional dispute. Particular attention should be given to the security situation around Baidoa, changes to Ethiopian and Egyptian troop arrangements, and Somalia’s political preparations ahead of the presidential election announced for May 15, 2027 . Diplomatic engagement through Kenya, IGAD or other regional mechanisms could become increasingly relevant if political divisions deepen. Whether mediation initiatives emerge, however, will depend on the willingness of the parties to pursue negotiation. Abiy’s Kenya visit ultimately illustrates the continuing value of dependable regional partnerships during a period of uncertainty. Ethiopia’s national interests require a stable Somalia, effective cooperation against Al Shabaab and security arrangements that do not unnecessarily entangle Ethiopian forces in domestic political rivalries. Its relationship with Kenya offers opportunities to advance those objectives while protecting economic integration and regional connectivity. The challenge for Addis Ababa is to preserve this partnership alongside constructive engagement with Mogadishu, ensuring that Somalia’s political disagreements do not become another source of confrontation across the Horn of Africa. بجد مع شركائه، وفي مقدمتهم الاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم وبقية الأندية، لتجاوز التحديات الراهنة وضمان استمرارية النشاط الرياضي وتطويره. كما شدد على أنّ المرحلة الحالية تتطلب من جميع الأطراف التحلي بروح football.summary: انتهت مباريات ذهاب دور الـ32 من دوري أبطال أفريقيا، حيث حقق الزمالك وبيراميدز انتصارات خارج ملعبهما، بينما واجه الترجي التونسي خسارة غير متوقعة. فاز بيراميدز على المريخ السوداني 1-0، وحقق الزمالك نفس النتيجة أمام الجيش الرواندي، مما يمنحهم أفضلية قبل الإياب. كما تألق يانج أفريكانز بفوز كبير 4-0 على سي إف إف إيه. في المقابل، خسر الترجي 1-0 أمام السويحلي الليبي، مما يعقد موقفه في مباراة العودة. شهدت المباريات الأخرى نتائج متنوعة، حيث تعادل النادي الإفريقي مع تي بي مازيمبي 1-1، وانتهت مباراة ماميلودي صن داونز مع ويليتي دي بالتعادل السلبي.

football.summary: اقترب فريق الهلال السوداني وفريق السويحلي الليبي من التأهل إلى دور المجموعات في دوري أبطال أفريقيا بعد أدائهما القوي في التصفيات. حيث حقق الهلال السوداني فوزاً مهماً على منافسه في مباراة الذهاب، مما يعزز فرصه في التأهل. من جهة أخرى، قدم السويحلي الليبي عرضاً مميزاً في مباراته، مما يضعه في موقف جيد للتقدم في البطولة. يتطلع كلا الفريقين إلى تحقيق نتائج إيجابية في مباريات الإياب لضمان مكانهما في دور المجموعات، حيث تعتبر هذه المرحلة من البطولة ذات أهمية كبيرة للأندية الأفريقية.
